lesson.title: Breaking the Confederacy's Will: Grant, Sherman, and Total War
lesson.summary: In 1864 and 1865, Ulysses S. Grant and William Tecumseh Sherman adopted a strategy of total war, targeting the Confederacy's economy, infrastructure, and civilian morale alongside its armies, a shift that finally brought the war to an end.
lesson.body:
By early 1864, the Union had won crucial victories at Gettysburg and Vicksburg, but the Confederacy, though badly weakened, was still fighting, and Lincoln needed a general willing to press that advantage relentlessly rather than retreat after a costly engagement, as several of his earlier commanders had done. In March 1864 Lincoln promoted Ulysses S. Grant, fresh off his successes in the western theater, to general in chief of all Union armies. Grant brought a different philosophy of war than his predecessors: rather than seeking a single decisive battle, he planned coordinated offensives on multiple fronts simultaneously, aiming to use the Union's larger population and industrial capacity to wear down Confederate armies through sustained, grinding pressure they could not match.

Grant's own campaign against Lee's Army of Northern Virginia in the summer of 1864, fought through the Wilderness, Spotsylvania Court House, and Cold Harbor, produced enormous casualties on both sides and drew sharp criticism in the North for its cost, but Grant refused to withdraw the way earlier Union commanders had after similarly bloody engagements. He instead kept pushing south, eventually pinning Lee's army into a prolonged siege at Petersburg, Virginia, beginning in June 1864, that would grind on for nearly ten months and steadily drain the Confederacy's remaining manpower and supplies.

At the same time, Grant gave General William Tecumseh Sherman command in the western theater with instructions to apply similar pressure against the Confederate heartland. Sherman captured Atlanta, an important rail and manufacturing center, in September 1864, a victory that gave a significant boost to Lincoln's reelection campaign that fall at a moment when war weariness in the North had made his defeat a real possibility. From Atlanta, Sherman marched roughly 60,000 troops across Georgia to Savannah between November and December 1864 in what became known as the March to the Sea, deliberately destroying railroads, factories, warehouses, and farms along a broad path in order to cripple the Confederacy's ability to supply its armies and to demonstrate to the Southern civilian population that its government could no longer protect them.

This approach, sometimes described as total war, marked a deliberate break from earlier conventions that tried to limit fighting mostly to opposing armies. Sherman and Grant reasoned that the Confederacy's ability to keep fighting depended as much on its railroads, farms, and civilian morale as on its soldiers, and that destroying that capacity would shorten the war and ultimately cost fewer lives than years of additional battles. Sherman continued the strategy into the Carolinas in early 1865, and combined with Grant's relentless pressure on Lee in Virginia, the Confederacy's capacity to resist collapsed within months. Lee finally abandoned Petersburg and Richmond in early April 1865 and surrendered to Grant at Appomattox Court House on April 9, 1865, effectively ending the Confederacy's ability to continue the war.
